All passing. Now let me think about a few more test scenarios that the hidden tests may include, especially around things my reference implements the same way (so fuzzing wouldn't catch a shared misreading). Let me re-read the protocol once more for any missed requirement, then finalize.

Re-reading key paragraphs:

"## Input and arithmetic ... All fractions below are pairs [p,q], integers 0<=p<=1000000,1<=q<=1000000; nonreduced input is allowed. Output fractions must be reduced with positive q." ✓ Fraction output is reduced ✓ positive denominator ✓.

"IDs match [A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,32}; string order is ASCII order." ✓ sorted() on Python strings = ASCII/codepoint order ✓.

"Root keys are exactly capacity, releases, blocks." ✓

"`blocks` is an array0..20000 of arrays of operations. Empty blocks are allowed. Flattening blocks defines zero-based operation indices at; block boundaries have no other effect." ✓

"A release has exactly: ... `packet_limit` (integer width..200000), `idle_us` (integer0..1000000000000)" ✓

"Every row has exactly `class` (integer0..classes-1), `values` (integer array)." ✓

"Discovery values have length2..128; other rows0..128." ✓

"A discovery array may be empty or omit classes." ✓

"Across the WHOLE request: discovery<=4096rows, train<=8192rows, validation<=8192rows, total values across these three arrays<=1048576, derived fragments<=4096, packets<=200000, opens<=8192, installs<=2048, and operations<=218432." ✓ all checked (fragments ✓ in pipeline).

"## Discovery certificate ... For each discovery row, define mean and population standard deviation of its activation values over the REAL prefix only." ✓

"Fragment IDs are zero-based discovery order: source-row order, then run order." ✓

"## Calibration and backup: ... No forced backup patterns are added when none survive." ✓ (no legacy backup-pattern forcing).

"Priority is decreasing EXACT score, then increasing cluster ID; it is shared across classes and lengths." ✓

"The backup certificate uses its native tree-node order." ✓

"## Tables and release banks ... The exact certificate entry count is min(actual distinct keys,capacity.exact+1). Only this clipped count is part of the certificate." ✓ 

Hmm — "Only this clipped count is part of the certificate" ✓ we only emit the count ✓.

"## Online behavior: Each epoch retains the release pinned at open, despite later successful installs." ✓

"Its first packet fixes positive direction: encoded feature is1514+length for that src,1514-length for the other." ✓

"Packet positions start at0 per epoch." ✓

"Timestamps must be nondecreasing within an epoch, even AFTER classification; there is no cross-flow or cross-epoch timestamp ordering requirement." ✓

"For an unclassified arriving packet, idle backup has precedence if at least width packets were already consumed and the gap from the previous packet is STRICTLY larger than idle_us: commit backup BEFORE consuming the new packet." ✓

"Otherwise consume it." ✓

"A segment match concerns a contiguous suffix ending at this packet, with enough REAL packets for its length. At the earliest packet with any match, commit the highest-priority matching cluster immediately. A future match cannot replace this decision." ✓

"If this packet has no match and the consumed count is STRICTLY greater than packet_limit, commit backup instead." ✓

"Backup always uses the FIRST width encoded features of the epoch, frozen once available." ✓ (I recompute the first width features at commit; equivalent since features only append.)

"At an unclassified close, right-pad a shorter prefix with1514 and commit backup, including a completely empty flow." ✓

"A gap before width packets does not classify or reset the epoch." ✓

"Idle is checked only on an arriving packet, not on close or a timer." ✓

"After commitment, packets bypass matching and backup, but timestamp validation and the open bank reference remain until close." ✓

"## Output certificate: Return exactly catalog, installs, decisions, final." ✓

"`catalog` follows release input order." ✓

"Each item has exactly: id, fragments, noise, clusters, priority, backup, entries" — wait, the item fields listed are: `id`, `fragments`, `noise`, `clusters` (with sub-fields), `priority`, `backup`, `entries` ✓ my catalog has exactly those 7 keys ✓.

"`clusters`, ordered by cluster ID." ✓

"`installs` follows install operation order. Each item has exactly at, id, status, resident, used" ✓

"`decisions` follows commitment order, exactly one per opened epoch. Each item: flow, epoch, release, at, seen, class, reason, rule, start" ✓ 9 keys ✓.

"`final` has exactly current, resident, used" ✓.

OK. One more thought on `seen` for the idle case: "seen counts packets consumed at commitment: idle excludes the arriving packet" ✓ = len(features) before appending ✓.

Now let me reconsider the risky interpretation: **"all opens must close by the end"** → invalid_request. Let me consider the alternative: it's a statement about the system (no automatic final close), and the request may end with open flows... but then "exactly one per opened epoch" fails. Also `close` "close an active epoch and release its bank reference" — the final state would keep those banks resident ✓ possible. Hmm.

The phrase is in the "Tables and release banks" section, right after "There is no automatic opening, expiry or final close". I read: "There is no automatic ... final close: all opens must close by the end [of the request]" — i.e., the request must close them itself. That's a rule on the request → violation = invalid_request ✓. I'll keep it.

Let me consider hedging: if an open never closes, I could still emit a decision... no; can't have both behaviors. Stick with invalid.

Next, one more consideration: `install` of a release ID that's supplied ✓ valid; a request with zero installs ✓ fine.

Another: what if `blocks` contains an op for a flow that was never opened but has an entry in `self.epochs`? Handled by flows dict ✓.

Another: `open` for a flow ID equal to a release ID → independent namespaces ✓.

Now let me think about the CPU time of `formats.validate` for the max request: 1.3s in the profile earlier (for a 10MB request) ✓ acceptable.

Also `check_containers` regex scan on 64MiB — let me measure the worst case: a 64MiB input. My fullbudget request is 10.4MB and the total validate was ~1.3s. For 64MiB (e.g. with big values arrays), the scan+parse might take ~8s. Acceptable.

Let me do a big-input test: a request with values totaling ~1M entries but few fragments — e.g. 8192 validation rows × 128 values = 1.05M values (the max) → JSON ~9MB. Hmm, the 64MiB bound is mostly about... discovery rows are ≤128 values and ≤4096 rows → 524k values; ops: 218432 ops ≈ maybe 10MB. So a legit request can't be huge (values ≤ 1.05M → ~9MB JSON). So 64MiB only matters for malformed input (rejected by container/op limits... hmm, malformed with many ops → ops limit triggers after parsing).

Let me test a large malformed input quickly (e.g. 60MB of ops) to check we don't blow the memory/time... The container scanner bounds depth/count ✓; parsing a 60MB JSON of ops would take ~10-20s and then reject on ops>218432 ✓ acceptable.

Now, let me double check memory for a worst-case valid request: RSS 282MB measured ✓ under 1GiB.

Let me now do a final look at rule_generate's clustering path for a subtle bug: in `cluster_group`, `sizes` is a concatenation of per-block column sums ✓ and `core = sizes >= minimum` ✓. For the noncore loop I use `_block_row(blocks, block, index)` with block=256 hardcoded ✓ (matches adjacency_of's block=256 default). Fragile coupling — let me pass the block size explicitly to avoid a future mismatch. Let me refactor: adjacency_of returns (blocks, sizes, block).

Also potential bug: `if count == 0: return [], np.zeros(0)` — handled by the caller (groups are non-empty) ✓.

Let me clean this up.
